meaning: The number 33 symbolizes the completion of a divine plan and is especially linked to Jesus' age at his crucifixion and resurrection, as well as to turning points in salvation history.
description: In Christian tradition, 33 is best known as the age at which Jesus Christ was crucified, died, and rose again, making the number a symbol of completed salvation and divine fulfillment. The number thus marks the culmination of God's plan of salvation – the point where suffering turns to victory. In Jewish tradition this motif is reflected in Lag BaOmer, the 33rd day of the Omer count, a festival that breaks a long period of mourning and marks a turning point from sorrow to joy. Thus, the number 33 carries deep symbolism in both traditions connected to divine completion and breakthrough.

versions.meaning: The number 33 symbolizes promises, the completion of a divine plan, and is especially linked to Jesus' age at his crucifixion and resurrection.
versions.description: In Christian tradition, 33 is best known as the age at which Jesus Christ was crucified, died, and rose again, making the number a symbol of completed salvation and divine perfection. In Jewish tradition, the 33rd day of the Omer count (Lag BaOmer) marks a festival that breaks a period of mourning, giving the number significance as a turning point from sorrow to joy. The name of God, Elohim, appears 33 times in the creation account in Genesis, linking the number to creative power and divine authority. King David also reigned for 33 years in Jerusalem, reinforcing the number's connection to kingship and divine rule.

footnotes.text: God's name Elohim appears, according to traditional Jewish counting, 33 times in the creation account (1 Mos 1:1–2:3), linking the number to creative power and divine authority. The exact count varies slightly depending on textual boundaries.
King David reigned for 33 years in Jerusalem (1 Kong 2:11), which reinforces the number's connection to kingship and divine governance in biblical history.

Lag BaOmer (the 33rd day of the Omer count) is celebrated, among other things, in memory of the end of a plague that struck Rabbi Akiva's students. The day is also linked to Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai's hillula (death anniversary), who according to tradition revealed deep mystical truths on this day.
